implementation_notes: Ktor Server ships the checkpoint as a first-party plugin: install(Authentication) registers named providers (basic, bearer/jwt, session, oauth) - the delegated, replaceable mechanism - and authenticate("name") wraps the routes that require identity. A provider's authenticate/validate callback receives a typed credential such as BearerTokenCredential and returns a Principal or null; route handlers read call.principal<UserIdPrincipal>() and never see credentials. Routes registered outside authenticate("...") remain public, so the protected set is explicit rather than framework-defaulted. Spring Boot with Kotlin instead uses the Java servlet filter chain, so choose the realization per stack.
pitfalls: Ktor has no default-deny: routes registered outside authenticate("...") are public, so the protected set must be deliberate and reviewed.
A blocking lookup (JDBC, file) inside the provider's validate callback blocks the event loop; use suspending clients or wrap in withContext(Dispatchers.IO).
